turns.content: right so – the caption. two sentences, dead simple, for a display case. i've got rosina harrison's line about the kitchen stove, and i want the label to carry that same kind of blunt fondness she had… my gran was a parlourmaid in cumbria and she'd've said exactly the same thing, you know? no airs and graces. so none of that "the oppressed servant bravely spoke truth to power" nonsense. just… two sentences that sound like someone who knew the job and liked the woman but wasn't having any of her nonsense. what've you got?
What’s Harrison’s exact line about the kitchen stove? Your gran’s “no airs and graces” gives me the tone: someone who knew the work, liked the woman, and wasn’t about to put her on a pedestal.
oh right sorry — the line is 'Haven't you forgotten the kitchen stove, my lady?' she says it when Lady Astor's trying on yet another necklace before some big dinner. so... yeah. that's the one.
Lady Astor was trying on yet another necklace before dinner when Rosina Harrison asked, “Haven’t you forgotten the kitchen stove, my lady?” There was dressing up, and then there was overdoing it.

oh brilliant — that's it, that's the tone. my gran would've snorted at that caption. can we move on to the audio guide bit? just a short note on why staff could get away with that kind of talk — like, what made it possible without getting the sack?

Glad it passes the gran test. For the audio, I’d keep that dryness but make clear that this wasn’t freedom every servant had:

“Not every servant could have got away with that. A lady’s maid worked closely with her employer, and familiarity, trust and being very good at the job could leave room for a sharp remark. Harrison’s quip gives us a glimpse of that latitude—not a licence for every servant to answer back.”

I’d frame it as room earned within a particular relationship, not proof that speaking freely carried no risk.

oh brilliant — yeah that audio note's spot on. the 'room earned within a particular relationship' bit is exactly it. my gran used to say 'you earn your mouth, or you hold it'... i'm stealing that for the display notes actually. okay next up — visitor handout card. need to explain 'everything but the kitchen stove' for foreign visitors. just the plain idiom gloss, nothing fancy.

“The usual English expression is ‘everything but the kitchen sink’: far more things than anyone needs. Harrison’s joke about the kitchen stove suggests that Lady Astor might as well wear that too, along with all her jewellery.”

oh perfect — yeah that's clean. the 'everything but the kitchen sink' gloss is exactly what foreign visitors need. no fuss. okay last thing then — the interpretive panel takeaway. one line that holds both sides: strict hierarchy but real familiarity. no melodrama, no nostalgia. just... the truth of it.
Strict hierarchy could coexist with real familiarity, but the freedom to speak plainly depended on the relationship.
